title: The Thumb at the Door
bigQuestion: A stranger arrives at Watson’s door before breakfast with his thumb cut off. What does he want, and why does Watson take him to Holmes?

mission.name: Pages 87 to 94
mission.blurb: A quick check that tonight’s reading landed — not a test.

practice.title: Watson, two years on
text: Of all the problems submitted to Sherlock Holmes, that of Mr. Hatherley’s thumb was so strange as to rank among the more remarkable — even if it gave my friend fewer opportunities for those deductive methods of reasoning by which he achieved such remarkable results.

It was in the summer of ’89, not long after my marriage, that the events occurred that I am about to summarize. I had returned to my practice and had abandoned Holmes in his Baker Street rooms, although I continually visited him.

My practice had steadily increased, and as I happened to live close to Paddington Station, I got a few patients from among the officials. One of these, whom I had cured of a painful and lingering disease, was constantly advertising my virtues.

waiting.title: Two men from Paddington
text: One morning, I was awakened by the maid tapping at the door, announcing that two men had come from Paddington and were waiting in the consulting room. I dressed hurriedly, for I knew by experience that railway cases were seldom trivial, and hastened downstairs.
“I’ve got him here,” he whispered, jerking his thumb over his shoulder. “He’s all right. I thought I’d bring him round myself; then he couldn’t slip away. There he is, all safe and sound.”

I entered my consulting-room and found a gentleman seated by the table. Round one of his hands he had a handkerchief wrapped, which was mottled all over with bloodstains. He was young, with a strong face, but he was exceedingly pale and looked like he was suffering from agitation.

“I am sorry to wake you, Doctor,” said he. “But I have had a very serious accident during the night. I came in by train this morning, and on inquiring as to where I might find a doctor, a worthy fellow escorted me here.”

card.title: The card, and the laugh
text: I glanced at it. “Mr. Victor Hatherley, hydraulic engineer, 16A Victoria Street (3rd floor).”

“I regret that I have kept you waiting,” said I, sitting down. “A night journey is a monotonous occupation.” “My night could not be called monotonous,” said he. He laughed very heartily, with a ringing note, leaning back in his chair and shaking his sides. All my medical instincts rose up against that laugh.
It was useless, however. He was off in one of those hysterical outbursts that come upon a strong nature when some great crisis is over. Presently he came to himself, very weary and blushing hotly.

thumb.title: Where the thumb used to be
text: “And now, Doctor, perhaps you would kindly attend to my thumb, or rather to the place where my thumb used to be.” He unwound the handkerchief and held out his hand.
There were four fingers and a horrid red spongy surface where the thumb should have been. It had been hacked or torn right out from the roots.

“Yes, it did. I fainted when it was done; and I think I must have been senseless for a long time. When I came to, I found that it was still bleeding, so I tied one end of my handkerchief very tightly round the wrist and braced it up with a twig.” “Excellent! You should have been a surgeon.” “It is a question of hydraulics, you see, and came within my own specialty.”

“This has been done,” said I, examining the wound, “by a very heavy and sharp instrument.” “A thing like a cleaver,” said he. “An accident, I presume?” “By no means.” “What, a murderous attack!” “Very murderous indeed.”

baker.title: To Baker Street
text: “I shall have to tell my tale to the police; but, if it were not for the evidence of this wound, I should be surprised if they believed my story, for it is very extraordinary, and I have not much proof with which to back it up. Even if they believe me, the clues I can give them are so vague that I doubt justice will ever be done.”
“If it is a problem that you desire to solve, I strongly recommend you come to my friend Mr. Sherlock Holmes before you go to the police.”

Sherlock Holmes was, as I expected, lounging about his sitting room in his dressing gown. He received us in his quietly genial fashion, ordered eggs, and joined us in a hearty meal. When it was concluded, he settled our new acquaintance upon the sofa and set a glass of brandy within his reach.
“It is easy to see that your experience has been no common one, Mr. Hatherley,” said he. “Pray lie down there and make yourself at home. Tell us what you can, but stop when you are tired.”

“I am an orphan and a bachelor, residing alone in lodgings in London. By profession I am a hydraulic engineer, with considerable experience during the seven years that I was apprenticed to Venner & Matheson, the well-known firm. Two years ago, having come into a fair sum of money through my poor father’s death, I decided to start in business for myself.”

items.hi: I had returned to my practice and had abandoned Holmes in his Baker Street rooms
items.q: By the summer of ’89 Watson is no longer living at Baker Street. Why not?
opts: He had married, and had gone back to his own medical practice
He had quarrelled with Holmes over the ending of a case
Holmes had asked him to leave while he worked alone
He had gone abroad for a year and had only just returned
items.why: It was the summer of ’89, not long after Watson’s marriage. He had returned to his practice and left Holmes in the Baker Street rooms — though he says he continually visited him, which is why he can still take a patient round there.

items.hi: as I happened to live close to Paddington Station, I got a few patients from among the officials
items.q: Why did Watson have patients who worked for the railway?
opts: He lived close to Paddington Station
He had once worked as a railway surgeon himself
The railway company paid him to treat its men
Holmes had sent the railway officials to him
items.why: He lived close to Paddington Station, so he picked up a few patients from among the officials there. One of them, cured of a painful and lingering disease, was constantly advertising Watson’s virtues — which is how a railway guard came to bring Hatherley to his door.

items.hi: I dressed hurriedly, for I knew by experience that railway cases were seldom trivial
items.q: The maid says two men have come from Paddington. Why does Watson dress in a hurry rather than take his time?
opts: He had learnt that railway cases were seldom trivial
The maid had told him that one of the men was bleeding
He was expecting Sherlock Holmes to call that morning
The guard had warned him that the man might slip away
items.why: Watson dressed hurriedly because he knew by experience that railway cases were seldom trivial. He had not seen the man or heard anything about him yet — the guard’s remark about slipping away comes later, on the stairs.

items.hi: I have had a very serious accident during the night. I came in by train this morning
items.q: He was hurt during the night and came in by train this morning. What does that tell you about where it happened?
opts: Well outside London, and hours before he found help
Somewhere in London, since he reached a doctor by the morning
At Paddington Station, which is why a railway guard brought him in
At his own lodgings, before he set out on the night train
items.why: Nothing in these pages says where he was. But he was hurt in the night, he fainted and lay senseless a long time, and he still had a train journey in front of him — so it happened well outside London, and hours passed before anyone looked at the wound. Holmes will want both of those facts.

items.hi: Mr. Victor Hatherley, hydraulic engineer, 16A Victoria Street (3rd floor).
items.q: What does the card the visitor left with the maid say he is?
opts: A hydraulic engineer
A railway guard
A surgeon
A watchmaker
items.why: The card reads: Mr. Victor Hatherley, hydraulic engineer, 16A Victoria Street (3rd floor). His trade matters twice over in these pages — it is how he explains his own first aid, and it is what the story turns on later.

items.hi: He was off in one of those hysterical outbursts that come upon a strong nature when some great crisis is over.
items.q: Watson says “A night journey is a monotonous occupation,” and Hatherley laughs until Watson shouts at him to stop. What does Watson say the laughing really was?
opts: A hysterical outburst, after a great crisis
A sign that he had invented the whole story
The effect of the brandy Watson had given him
A joke he had been saving up for the doctor
items.why: Watson calls it one of those hysterical outbursts that come upon a strong nature when some great crisis is over — so the laugh is evidence of what he has been through, not of high spirits. The brandy comes afterwards, to bring his colour back.

hi: I tied one end of my handkerchief very tightly round the wrist and braced it up with a twig
It is a question of hydraulics, you see, and came within my own specialty.
items.q: Hatherley fainted, and when he came round the wound was still bleeding. What had he done about it by the time he reached Watson?
opts: Tied his handkerchief round the wrist, tightened with a twig
Held his hand above his head for the whole journey to London
Packed the wound with cloth torn from his own coat
Nothing at all, until the railway guard bound it for him
items.why: He made a tourniquet: the handkerchief tied tightly round the wrist and braced up with a twig. Watson says he should have been a surgeon, and Hatherley answers that it is a question of hydraulics and came within his own specialty — he solved it as an engineer.

items.hi: It is a question of hydraulics, you see, and came within my own specialty.
items.q: Watson says he should have been a surgeon. Hatherley answers that it was “a question of hydraulics … within my own specialty.” What does he mean by that?
opts: Stopping blood is the same problem as stopping flow in a pipe
He had been taught first aid as part of his engineering training
He had worked as a surgeon before he turned to engineering
He had read about tourniquets in an engineering journal once
items.why: A hydraulic engineer’s whole trade is controlling something that flows through a narrow space under pressure. He did not need medical training to know that squeezing the pipe above the leak would stop it — he already knew the shape of that problem, and the shape is the same whether the pipe is a hose or an arm.

hi: “An accident, I presume?” “By no means.” “What, a murderous attack!” “Very murderous indeed.”
items.q: Watson assumes the thumb was lost in an accident. What does Hatherley tell him?
opts: That it was a murderous attack
That a machine had caught his hand
That it happened while he was asleep
That he cannot remember how it happened
items.why: “An accident, I presume?” “By no means.” “What, a murderous attack!” “Very murderous indeed.” Watson had already worked out that the wound was made by a very heavy and sharp instrument, and Hatherley names it: a thing like a cleaver.

items.hi: the clues I can give them are so vague that I doubt justice will ever be done
items.q: Hatherley means to go to the police as well as to Holmes. What is he afraid the police will not manage?
opts: The clues he can give are too vague for justice to be done
They will blame him for bringing the injury on himself
They will stop him from going back to his own work
They will hand his name straight to the newspapers
items.why: Without the wound he doubts they would believe him at all, and even if they do, the clues he can give are so vague that he doubts justice will ever be done. That is the gap Holmes is for — and Holmes settles him on the sofa with brandy and tells him to stop when he is tired.

hi: he settled our new acquaintance upon the sofa and set a glass of brandy within his reach
Tell us what you can, but stop when you are tired.
items.q: Holmes orders breakfast, settles Hatherley on the sofa with brandy, and tells him to stop when he is tired — all before hearing a word. Why go to that trouble first?
opts: A steadied man tells it better, and Holmes wants the story straight
Holmes is hungry, and will not be interrupted before he has eaten
Holmes has already guessed the story and is in no hurry to hear it
Holmes is waiting for the police to arrive before anything is said
items.why: This is the same man who was laughing hysterically at Watson’s door an hour ago. Holmes wants evidence, and evidence out of an exhausted witness comes out muddled — so he feeds him, lies him down, puts the brandy where he can reach it, and tells him he may stop. It looks like kindness, and it is, but it is also how you get a clean account.

title: Fifty Guineas and a Promise
bigQuestion: Colonel Lysander Stark offers an hour’s work for fifty guineas. What is he really paying for — and what does Hatherley notice but go anyway?

mission.name: Pages 95 to 103
mission.blurb: A quick check that tonight’s reading landed — not a test.

den.title: Two years in a little den
text: During two years I have had only three consultations and one small job. Every day, from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon, I waited in my little den, until my heart began to sink, and I came to think I should never have any practice at all.

“Yesterday, however, my clerk entered to say there was a gentleman waiting to see me upon business. He brought a card, too, with the name of ‘Colonel Lysander Stark’ engraved upon it. At his heels came the Colonel himself. I do not think that I have ever seen so thin a man. His whole face sharpened away into nose and chin. Yet this thinness seemed to be natural, and due to no disease, for his eye was bright, his step brisk, and his bearing assured. He was plainly but neatly dressed, and his age, I judge, would be near forty.”

secret.title: The promise
text: “‘You have been recommended to me as a man who is not only proficient in his profession, but is also capable of preserving a secret.’”

“I bowed, feeling as flattered as any young man would at such a greeting. ‘May I ask who it was who gave me so good a reference?’ I asked. ‘Well, perhaps it is better that I should not tell you just at this moment. I have it from the same source that you are both an orphan and a bachelor, and you are residing alone in London.’”

“‘I have a professional commission for you, but absolute secrecy is essential – absolute secrecy, you understand, and of course we may expect that more from a man who lives alone than from one who lives in the bosom of his family.’”

“He looked hard at me as I spoke, and I have never seen so suspicious and questioning an eye. ‘Absolute and complete silence, before, during, and after? No reference to the matter at all, either in word or writing?’”

offer.title: Fifty guineas
text: “A feeling of repulsion and fear had begun to rise within me at the antics of this fleshless man.”

“‘How would fifty guineas for a night’s work suit you?’ he asked. ‘Most admirably.’ ‘I say a night’s work. But an hour’s would be nearer the mark. I simply want your opinion about a hydraulic stamping machine that has gotten out of gear. If you show us what is wrong, we shall set it right ourselves. What do you think?’ ‘The work appears to be light, and the pay generous.’”

“‘We shall want you to come tonight by the last train to Eyford, in Berkshire. It is a little place near the borders of Oxfordshire. There is a train from Paddington that would bring you in there at about eleven fifteen. I shall come down in a carriage to meet you.’”

night.title: Why so late
text: “‘Yes, our little place is in the country. It is a good seven miles from Eyford station.’ ‘Then we can hardly get there before midnight. I suppose there would be no chance of a train back. I should be forced to stop for the night.’ ‘Yes, we could easily give you a shakedown.’”

“‘We judge it best that you should come late. It is to recompense you for any inconvenience that we are paying you, an unknown man, a fee that would buy an opinion from the very heads of your profession. Of course, if you would like to get out of this business, there is time to do so.’”
“I thought of the fifty guineas, and of how very useful they would be to me. ‘Not at all,’ said I; ‘I should like, however, to understand a little more clearly what it is that you wish me to do.’”

earth.title: Fuller’s earth
vocab: A clay used in manufacturing processes.
text: “‘You may be aware that fuller’s earth is a valuable product, and that it is only found in one or two places in England?’”

“‘Some little time ago I bought a small place within ten miles of Reading. I was fortunate to discover that there was a deposit of fuller’s earth in one of my fields. On examining it, however, I found that this deposit formed a link between two very much larger ones – both of them in the grounds of my neighbors. These good people did not know that their land contained that which was quite as valuable as a gold mine. Naturally, it was to my interest to buy their land before they discovered its true value; but I had no money by which I could do this.’”

“‘I took a few of my friends into the secret, however, and they suggested that we should secretly work our own little deposit, and in this way earn the money to buy the neighboring fields. This we have now been doing for some time, and to help us in our operations we erected a hydraulic press. This press, as I have already explained, has gotten out of order, and we wish your advice.’”

press.title: A mere detail
text: “‘The only point that I could not quite understand,’ said I, ‘was what use you could make of a hydraulic press in excavating fuller’s earth, which, as I understand, is dug out from a pit.’”

“‘Ah!’ said he carelessly, ‘we have our own process. We compress the earth into bricks, so as to remove them without revealing what they are. But that is a mere detail. I have taken you fully into my confidence, now, Mr. Hatherley, and I have shown you how I trust you.’ He rose as he spoke. ‘I shall expect you, then, at Eyford, at 11:15.’ ‘I shall certainly be there.’ ‘And not a word to a soul.’ He looked at me with a last long, questioning gaze, and then he hurried from the room.”

weigh.title: Throwing his fears to the winds
text: “On the one hand, of course, I was glad, for the fee was at least ten times what I should have asked had I set a price on my own services, and this order might lead to other ones. On the other hand, my patron had made an unpleasant impression upon me, and I could not think that his explanation was sufficient to explain the necessity for my coming at midnight, and his extreme anxiety least I should tell anyone of my errand.”
“However, I threw my fears to the winds, ate a hearty supper, drove to Paddington, and started off, having obeyed to the letter the order to hold my tongue.”

arrival.title: The carriage at Eyford
text: “I was in time for the last train to Eyford, and I reached the little station after eleven o’clock. I was the only passenger who got out there, and there was no one upon the platform. As I passed out the gate, however, I found my acquaintance of the morning waiting in the shadow. Without a word he grasped my arm and hurried me into a carriage. He drew up the windows on either side and away we went, as hard as the horse could go.”
“One horse?” interjected Holmes. “Yes, only one.” “Did you observe the color?” “Yes, it was a chestnut.”

items.hi: During two years I have had only three consultations and one small job
items.q: Hatherley begins by telling Holmes how little work he has had in two years. Why start there?
opts: It explains why he took a job he did not like the look of
It explains why he was still at his desk so late that evening
It explains why he had never heard of Colonel Lysander Stark
It explains why he had no clerk to send out on the errand
items.why: Three consultations and one small job in two years, and a heart that sank a little further every afternoon. Fifty guineas is not a temptation to a busy man. Hatherley is telling Holmes what the money meant to him before he tells him what he did for it.

items.hi: this thinness seemed to be natural, and due to no disease, for his eye was bright, his step brisk, and his bearing assured
items.q: Hatherley says he never saw so thin a man, but that the thinness was natural and not from illness. What made him sure of that?
opts: A bright eye, a brisk step and an assured bearing
The Colonel said so himself when he introduced his business
The good cut and quality of the clothes he was wearing
He was too young for any serious illness to have taken hold
items.why: Hatherley is a careful observer, which is what makes him a good witness later. A sick man is dull-eyed and slow; this one was bright, brisk and assured, so the thinness had to be his ordinary build.

items.hi: we may expect that more from a man who lives alone than from one who lives in the bosom of his family
items.q: Stark knows Hatherley is an orphan, a bachelor, and living alone. What reason does he give for caring about that?
opts: A man who lives alone can keep a secret better than one with a family
A man who lives alone can travel at short notice without explaining
A man who lives alone will work for less than one with a family
A man who lives alone has no one to worry if he is out all night
items.why: That is the reason he gives, and it sounds almost reasonable. Notice what sits either side of it: he will not say who recommended Hatherley, but that same unnamed source told him exactly who has nobody at home. He came knowing.

items.hi: Absolute and complete silence, before, during, and after? No reference to the matter at all, either in word or writing?
items.q: Stark asks for silence “before, during, and after … either in word or writing.” Which part of that is the odd one?
opts: After — once a machine is mended there is nothing left to hide
Before — nobody could tell a secret they had not yet been told
In word — a spoken promise cannot be checked either way
In writing — an engineer must keep notes to do the work at all
items.why: Before and during protect a business secret, and a jealously guarded deposit is a fair thing to protect. Afterwards is different: once the press is mended there is nothing left to give away, unless what needs covering is not the fuller’s earth but the evening itself. And no reference in writing means no record anywhere that he ever went.

items.hi: I simply want your opinion about a hydraulic stamping machine that has gotten out of gear
items.q: What is the work Stark actually asks for?
opts: An opinion on a hydraulic stamping machine that is out of gear
The repair of a hydraulic press that has broken down
The design of a new machine for a business in the country
A survey of a field to value the clay lying under it
items.why: An opinion, not a repair: “If you show us what is wrong, we shall set it right ourselves.” An hour’s work, by Stark’s own reckoning. Fifty guineas for an hour of talking is the first figure in this story that does not add up.

items.hi: There is a train from Paddington that would bring you in there at about eleven fifteen
items.q: What travelling does Stark ask him to do?
opts: The last train to Eyford, arriving about a quarter past eleven
The first train to Reading, arriving early the next morning
A carriage the whole way from London, leaving after supper
The last train to Oxford, where a carriage would be waiting
items.why: Eyford, in Berkshire, on the last train from Paddington, in at about 11:15, with Stark meeting the train in a carriage. Hold on to the time and the place — Holmes will want both, and so will you.

items.hi: Yes, we could easily give you a shakedown.
items.q: Stark offers Hatherley a shakedown for the night. What is a shakedown?
opts: A makeshift bed
A hot meal before the journey home
A ride back to the station at dawn
An extra payment for the trouble
items.why: A makeshift bed — something thrown together on the floor rather than a proper guest room. Hatherley has just worked out that he cannot get back to London that night, and the offer is made easily, as though it had been expected.

items.hi: We judge it best that you should come late.
items.q: Hatherley asks whether he could come at a more convenient hour. What does Stark actually give as his reason for the late arrival?
opts: None — he says only that they judge it best, then mentions the fee
That the machine can only be stopped once the day’s work is done
That the neighbours would see a stranger arriving in daylight
That the last train is the only one that stops at Eyford at all
items.why: He gives no reason at all. “We judge it best that you should come late” — and then straight on to the money, and to the offer of a way out if he does not like it. The third answer above is a reason Stark could have given and did not; brushing past the question is the point.

items.hi: These good people did not know that their land contained that which was quite as valuable as a gold mine.
items.q: Why does Stark say he wants to work his own small deposit of fuller’s earth in secret?
opts: To buy his neighbours’ land before they learn its value
To avoid paying the tax that is owed on a working clay pit
To keep a rival company from opening a pit of its own nearby
To stop his friends from claiming a larger share of the profits
items.why: Fuller’s earth is a clay used in manufacturing, and it is found in only one or two places in England. Stark’s field links two much larger deposits on either side, and the neighbours do not know what they are standing on. He tells this part readily enough, and it is not a flattering story to tell about himself.

items.hi: was what use you could make of a hydraulic press in excavating fuller’s earth, which, as I understand, is dug out from a pit
items.q: Hatherley asks what use a hydraulic press could be in digging clay out of a pit. Why is that such a good question?
opts: A press squeezes things; it is no use for digging them up
A press would be far too expensive for so small a business
A press cannot be worked without a much larger water supply
A press would crack the clay and spoil it before it was sold
items.why: It is the one question an engineer would ask and a liar would not expect, because the tool does not fit the job. Watch how it is answered: “Ah!” said he carelessly — bricks, to carry the stuff away unrecognised — “but that is a mere detail.” The only thing in the whole account that does not hold together is waved off as a detail, and Stark stands up and leaves before it can be asked again.

hi: I could not think that his explanation was sufficient to explain the necessity for my coming at midnight
However, I threw my fears to the winds
items.q: By the end of the evening Hatherley has worked out for himself that the story does not hold. What does he do about it?
opts: Nothing — he puts his fears aside and goes
He writes the address down and leaves it with his clerk
He decides to go, but to ask for half the fee in advance
He calls at the police station on his way to Paddington
items.why: He lists the very doubts a reader has been collecting — the unpleasant impression, the midnight hour, the anxiety about his telling anyone — and then throws them to the winds, eats a hearty supper and catches the train. He also keeps the promise to the letter, so not one person knows where he has gone. That is the sentence to remember when you read on.

hi: I was the only passenger who got out there, and there was no one upon the platform
He drew up the windows on either side and away we went
items.q: At Eyford, Stark takes his arm without a word and at once draws up the windows on both sides of the carriage. What is the likeliest reason?
opts: So that Hatherley cannot see where he is being taken
So that the night air does not chill a tired traveller
So that nobody on the road can recognise the Colonel
So that the noise of the wheels does not drown their talk
items.why: He was the only passenger to get off, the platform was empty, and Stark was waiting in the shadow rather than in the light. Then the windows go up before a word is spoken. A closed carriage on a dark road means Hatherley cannot say afterwards where he went — which is exactly why Holmes starts asking about the horse.

title: The Machine and the Circle
bigQuestion: Hatherley is warned twice and stays, and nearly dies for it. By the end, four men are pointing at four different places on a map — and Holmes says all four are wrong. What did Hatherley see that none of them have used yet?

horse.title: Holmes stops him to ask about the horse
text: Without a word he grasped my arm and hurried me into a carriage.
He drew up the windows on either side and away we went, as hard as the horse could go.
“One horse?” interjected Holmes.
“Yes, only one.”
“Did you observe the color?”
“Yes, it was a chestnut.”
“Tired-looking or fresh?”
“Oh, fresh and glossy.”
“Thank you. Pray continue your tale.”

drive.title: An hour in the dark, and no way to see out
text: We drove for at least an hour.
Colonel Stark had said that it was only seven miles, but I think that it must have been nearer twelve.
He sat in silence all the time, and I was aware that he was looking at me with great intensity.
I tried to look out of the windows to see something of where we were, but they were made of frosted glass, and I could make out nothing except an occasional blur of passing light.
Now and then I hazarded some remark to break the boredom of the journey, but the Colonel answered only in grunts.

warn.title: “There is no good for you to do”
text: An uneasiness began to steal over me.
Who were these German people, and what were they doing living in this strange, out-of-the-way place?
And where was the place?
I was ten miles or so from Eyford, that was all I knew.
I could see that she was sick with fear, and the sight sent a chill to my own heart.
She held up one shaking finger to warn me to be silent, and she shot a few words of broken English at me, her eyes glancing back into the gloom behind her.
“I would go,” said she, trying hard to speak calmly. “There is no good for you to do.”
“It is not worth your while to wait,” she went on. “You can pass through the door; no one hinders.”

plea.title: She asks a second time, and he stays anyway
text: “For the love of Heaven!” she whispered, “get away before it is too late!”
But I am somewhat headstrong by nature.
I thought of my fifty-guinea fee, of my wearisome journey, and the unpleasant night that seemed to be before me.
Was it all for nothing?
Why should I slink away without having carried out my commission, and without the payment that was my due?
With a stout bearing, therefore, I declared my intention of remaining where I was.

inside.title: “We are now actually within the hydraulic press”
text: “We are now,” said he, “actually within the hydraulic press, and it would be particularly unpleasant for us if anyone were to turn it on.”
“The ceiling of this small chamber is really the end of the descending piston, and it comes down with the force of many tons upon this metal floor.”
When I pressed down the levers that controlled it, I knew at once by the whishing sound that there was a slight leakage.
An examination showed that one of the rubber bands around the end of a driving-rod had shrunk so as not quite to fill the socket along which it worked.
This was clearly the cause of the loss of power, and I pointed it out to my companions, who asked several practical questions as to how they should set it right.

trough.title: The crust in the iron trough, and one question too many
text: It was obvious that the story of the fuller’s earth was a fabrication, for it would be absurd to suppose that so powerful an engine could be designed for so small a purpose.
The walls were of wood, but the floor consisted of a large iron trough, and I could see a crust of metallic deposit all over it.
I was scraping at it to see exactly what it was, when I heard an exclamation in German, and saw the ghostly face of the Colonel looking down at me.
“I think that I would be better able to advise you as to your machine,” said I, “if I knew what the exact purpose was for which it was used.”
The instant that I uttered the words I regretted the rashness of my speech.
A sinister light sprang up in his grey eyes.
“Very well,” said he, “you shall know all about the machine.”
He took a step backward, slammed the door, and turned the key in the lock.

ceiling.title: The ceiling comes down
text: And then suddenly in the silence I heard the clank of the levers and the swish of the leaking cylinder.
He had set the engine at work.
By its light I saw that the black ceiling was coming down on me, slowly, jerkily, but, as none knew better than myself, with a force that must grind me to a shapeless pulp.
I begged the Colonel to let me out, but the remorseless clanking of the levers drowned my cries.
The ceiling was only a foot or two above my head, and with my hand I could feel its hard rough surface.
Already I was unable to stand erect, when my eye caught something that brought a gush of hope back.

panel.title: Iron above and below, wood at the sides
text: Though the floor and ceiling were of iron, the walls were of wood.
As I gave a last hurried glance around, I saw a thin line of yellow light between two of the boards, which broadened as a small panel was pushed backwards.
I could hardly believe that here was indeed a door that led away from death.
I threw myself through it and lay half fainting upon the other side.
The panel had closed again behind me, but the clang of the two slabs of metal told me how narrow had been my escape.

fritz.title: “Remember your promise after the last time”
text: She threw her arms round him and tried to hold him back.
“Fritz! Fritz!” she cried in English, “remember your promise after the last time. You said it would not happen again. He will be silent!”
“You are mad, Elise!” he shouted, struggling to break away from her. “You will be the ruin of us. He has seen too much.”
He dashed her to one side, and, rushing to the window, cut at me with his heavy weapon.
I was hanging with my hands across the sill when his blow fell.
I glanced at my hand, which was throbbing painfully, and, for the first time, saw that my thumb had been cut off.

hedge.title: Where he wakes up
text: It must have been a long time, for a bright morning was breaking when I came to myself.
My clothes were all wet with dew, and my coat-sleeve was drenched with blood.
But, to my astonishment, neither house nor garden were to be seen.
I had been lying in an angle of the hedge close by the road, and just a little lower down was the very train station at which I had arrived the previous night.

advert.title: The engineer who went out at ten o’clock and never came back
text: Then Sherlock Holmes pulled from the shelf one of the books in which he placed his newspaper cuttings.
“Here is an advertisement that will interest you,” said he. “It appeared in all the papers about a year ago.”
“Lost on the 9th inst., Mr. Jeremiah Hayling, aged 26, a hydraulic engineer. Left his lodgings at ten o’clock at night, and has not been heard of since.”
“Ha! That represents the last time the Colonel needed his machine overhauled, I fancy.”
“Good heavens!” cried my patient. “Then that explains what the girl said.”
“Undoubtedly. It is clear that the Colonel was a cool and desperate man, who was absolutely determined that nothing should stand in the way of his little game.”

guesses.title: Four guesses, and Holmes says all four are wrong
text: “I think I could lay my finger on it,” said Holmes quietly.
“I say it is south, for the country is more deserted there.”
“And I say east,” said my patient.
“I am for the west,” remarked the plain-clothes man. “There are quiet little villages up there.”
“And I am for the north,” said I; “because there are no hills there, and our friend says that he did not notice the carriage go up any.”
“You are all wrong.”
“But we can’t all be.”
“Oh, yes, you can.”

missions.name: Chapter 1 — pages 103 to 107
missions.blurb: The drive out, the dark house, and a warning he does not take

hi: fresh and glossy
as hard as the horse could go

vs.q: Holmes interrupts the story to ask the horse’s colour and whether it looked tired. Why is that worth interrupting for?
opts: A horse fresh and glossy cannot just have done a long drive
A chestnut horse would be easy for the police to trace
It shows which stable in Eyford the carriage was hired from
One horse means the household could not afford a second
vs.why: Holmes is not making conversation. Hatherley believes he was driven a long way; a horse that comes back fresh and glossy has not been driven a long way. It is the first crack in the story, and Holmes finds it before Hatherley has finished telling it.

vs.q: Hatherley says the horse was a chestnut, fresh and glossy. What does that quietly contradict?
opts: The Colonel’s claim to be short of ready money
The hour at which the train reached Eyford
The length of the drive he had just been taken on
The direction in which the carriage set off
vs.why: The drive is the thing it contradicts. Hatherley thinks he went nearer twelve miles; the horse says otherwise. Notice that Hatherley reports the fact without seeing what it means — he is a good witness and Holmes is a good listener.

vs.q: Of everything so far, Holmes stops him only to ask about the horse. What does that show about the way Holmes listens?
opts: He is more interested in horses than in the machine
He picks out the one detail that can be checked against another
He wants Hatherley to slow down so that Watson can take notes
He always asks about whatever came first in a story
vs.why: A story can be argued with; a tired horse cannot. Holmes reaches for the detail that can be tested against something else in the account, and lets the rest of the tale run on.

vs.q: Which of Hatherley’s answers is the one Holmes was really fishing for?
opts: That there was only one horse
That the horse was a chestnut
That they went as hard as the horse could go
That the horse was fresh and glossy
vs.why: The colour and the number are ordinary questions that make the last one sound ordinary too. Fresh and glossy is the answer that matters, and it is the one Holmes asks for last.

vs.q: Suppose the horse had come back tired and lathered instead. What would Holmes have learned?
opts: That the Colonel had borrowed the horse for the night
That the drive really had been long, and the house really far off
That the roads around Eyford were in poor repair
That the carriage must have stopped somewhere along the road
vs.why: Turn the clue round and you can see what it is worth. A tired horse would have supported Hatherley’s twelve miles. A fresh one denies it, and that is why Holmes asked.

hi: nearer twelve
frosted glass
answered only in grunts

vs.q: Stark had said the house was seven miles from the station. What did the drive actually feel like to Hatherley?
opts: Rather less than seven miles, taken slowly
About seven miles, just as he had been told
At least an hour, and nearer twelve miles
Two hours or more, over very steep ground
vs.why: “We drove for at least an hour. Colonel Stark had said that it was only seven miles, but I think that it must have been nearer twelve.” Remember it: this estimate is the one thing everybody later builds on, and it is a guess made in the dark.

vs.q: Why could Hatherley not see where he was being driven?
opts: The windows were made of frosted glass
The Colonel had made him promise to keep his eyes shut
A blanket had been thrown over the carriage windows
It was too dark outside to make out anything at all
vs.why: Frosted glass — so he could see “nothing except an occasional blur of passing light.” It is not simply that the night was dark: the carriage was built so that a passenger could not look out of it.

vs.q: How does the Colonel behave during the hour in the carriage?
opts: He questions Hatherley closely about his family
He talks cheerfully to keep his guest at ease
He falls asleep almost as soon as they set off
He says almost nothing, and watches Hatherley closely
vs.why: He sat in silence, looking at Hatherley “with great intensity,” and answered attempts at conversation “only in grunts.” A man taking an engineer to a job does not need to watch him for an hour.

vs.q: Hatherley’s guess of nearly twelve miles turns out to matter a great deal later. Why should you treat it carefully?
opts: He was counting the miles aloud to himself as they drove along
The Colonel told him the distance twice over
It is a guess made in the dark with nothing to check it against
He had travelled the same road earlier that day
vs.why: He could not see out, he did not know the roads, and he was jolted about for an hour. Everything he says about the distance rests on how long it felt — which is exactly the sort of evidence Holmes does not trust.

vs.q: Put the two facts together: an hour of jolting, and nothing to see. What was the drive designed to do?
opts: Tire Hatherley out before he had to work
Leave him with no idea where the house was
Give the household time to hide the machine
Keep him from being seen by anyone on the road
vs.why: Frosted windows, an hour of silence and a driver going as hard as the horse could go. Whatever else the drive achieved, it made sure the passenger could never find the place again — or lead anyone back to it.

hi: There is no good for you to do
no one hinders
sick with fear
ten miles or so from Eyford

vs.q: The woman comes to the door of his room. What does she tell him to do?
opts: To go, because there is no good for him to do there
To hide until the Colonel has gone to bed
To take the lamp and look at the upstairs rooms
To say nothing about having seen her at all
vs.why: “I would go... There is no good for you to do.” She says it in broken English, looking back into the dark behind her, shaking. She is risking a great deal to say it.

vs.q: She adds, “You can pass through the door; no one hinders.” Why does she bother to say that?
opts: To prove she has not locked him in herself
To show him she knows the house better than he does
To tell him the way out is open now and may not stay open
To make him think the Colonel has gone out
vs.why: She is not describing the door, she is offering him a chance. Nobody is watching the hall yet. In a few minutes the newcomers arrive on the stairs, and it is too late.

vs.q: What does Hatherley notice about the woman herself as she speaks?
opts: That she was angry with him for coming
That she was sick with fear
That she was dressed to leave the house
That she had been crying before she came in
vs.why: “I could see that she was sick with fear, and the sight sent a chill to my own heart.” The warning is frightening because of the state of the person giving it, and he feels that — then stays anyway.

vs.q: He asks himself where he is. What is the only answer he can give?
opts: Somewhere south of Reading
About seven miles from Eyford
Ten miles or so from Eyford, and nothing more
Within an hour’s walk of the police station
vs.why: “I was ten miles or so from Eyford, that was all I knew.” Hold on to that sentence. Every search later in the story is built on this one shaky guess of his.

vs.q: She warns him at real risk to herself, and he stays. What does that tell you about him?
opts: He does not believe a word she says
He thinks the Colonel will protect him
He is brave, and stubborn about finishing what he took on
He has not understood a single word of her broken English
vs.why: He understood her perfectly — he calls himself “somewhat headstrong” a page later and admits he rejected her warning foolishly. It is courage and obstinacy at once, and it nearly kills him.

missions.name: Chapter 2 — pages 108 to 111
missions.blurb: Ferguson, the machine, and the one question he should not have asked

hi: For the love of Heaven
somewhat headstrong by nature
my fifty-guinea fee

vs.q: She asks a second time, with her hands together: “get away before it is too late!” What does Hatherley do?
opts: Promises to go as soon as he has seen the machine
Declares that he intends to stay where he is
Asks her to explain what the danger is
Goes out to the hall to look for the front door
vs.why: “With a stout bearing, therefore, I declared my intention of remaining where I was.” Not a moment of doubt on the outside — though he has just listed to himself all the reasons he is staying.

vs.q: What reasons does Hatherley give himself for staying?
opts: That the Colonel would come after him if he ran
That he had promised the doctor he would finish the job
That he could not find his way back in the dark
His fee, his long journey, and the work he had taken on
vs.why: “I thought of my fifty-guinea fee, of my wearisome journey, and the unpleasant night that seemed to be before me. Was it all for nothing?” The money is first on the list — he is honest about that.

vs.q: How does Hatherley describe his own character at this moment?
opts: As somewhat headstrong by nature
As slow to take fright
As a poor judge of people
As too polite to argue with a lady
vs.why: “But I am somewhat headstrong by nature.” He is telling this to Holmes after the event, so he already knows how it turned out, and he does not excuse himself.

vs.q: What interrupts the woman before she can plead with him again?
opts: A door slams and footsteps come up the stairs
The Colonel calls her name from the hall
The lamp on the table goes out
Someone begins knocking at the front door
vs.why: “A door slammed, and the sound of several footsteps was heard upon the stairs.” She listens, throws up her hands “with a despairing gesture,” and is gone. The chance she offered him closes in that instant.

vs.q: Twice now she has told him to go, and twice he has refused. What is the story doing by repeating it?
opts: Showing that she is not to be trusted
Making it clear that what happens next is his own choice
Hinting that she wants the fee for herself
Suggesting that she is only trying to delay him a little
vs.why: He is not tricked into the danger and he is not dragged into it. He is warned, plainly, twice, and walks in — which is why he calls his own advice-rejecting “foolish” when he looks back on it.

hi: actually within the hydraulic press
the end of the descending piston
a slight leakage
had shrunk so as not quite to fill the socket

vs.q: Where is Hatherley standing while the Colonel explains the machine?
opts: In a gallery looking down on it
Inside the hydraulic press itself
In the corridor outside the little room
On a platform above the metal floor
vs.why: “We are now actually within the hydraulic press.” The room is the machine. Stark even says it would be “particularly unpleasant for us if anyone were to turn it on” — and twenty minutes later he turns it on himself.

vs.q: What is the ceiling of the little room?
opts: A trap door to the floor above
The end of the descending piston
A sheet of iron holding up the water tank
The underside of the main water columns
vs.why: “The ceiling of this small chamber is really the end of the descending piston, and it comes down with the force of many tons upon this metal floor.” Hatherley is told exactly how he is meant to die, as a piece of engineering.

vs.q: How does Hatherley first know something is wrong with the machine?
opts: A whishing sound when he pressed down the levers
The piston came down more slowly than it should
Water was standing on the metal floor
The levers would not move at all
vs.why: He hears it before he sees it — “I knew at once by the whishing sound that there was a slight leakage.” That leak comes back later: it is the swish he hears through the door when the engine is set at work.

vs.q: What exactly had gone wrong with the press?
opts: A driving-rod had bent out of true
The metal floor had cracked somewhere under the pressure
One of the water columns had sprung a leak
A rubber band had shrunk and no longer filled its socket
vs.why: “One of the rubber bands around the end of a driving-rod had shrunk so as not quite to fill the socket along which it worked.” A small fault, found in minutes. He really was worth his fee, which is part of what makes the evening so ugly.

vs.q: Stark says it would be unpleasant for them if anyone turned the machine on while they stood in it. Why does that line matter so much later?
opts: Because Ferguson is the one who works the levers
Because it is exactly what Stark does to him
Because it explains why the room is so small
Because it warns Hatherley to keep away from the levers
vs.why: It is said as a joke about their own safety. Within the hour Stark locks that door and sets the engine going with Hatherley inside — and Hatherley, who has just examined it, knows better than anyone what is coming down.

hi: a crust of metallic deposit
was a fabrication
if I knew what the exact purpose was
turned the key in the lock

vs.q: What convinces Hatherley that the fuller’s earth story is untrue?
opts: The house had no clay anywhere in it
Ferguson admitted there was no pit
So powerful an engine could not be for so small a purpose
The Colonel could not say where the clay pit actually was
vs.why: “It would be absurd to suppose that so powerful an engine could be designed for so small a purpose.” He reasons it out from the machine itself, as an engineer would, and he is right.

vs.q: What does he find on the floor of the machine?
opts: A large iron trough with a crust of metallic deposit
Several pounds of pale clay, freshly dug
Scratches where something heavy had been dragged
A pool of oil leaking from the driving-rod
vs.why: Metal, not clay. He is scraping at the crust to see what it is when the Colonel appears above him — and the crust is the real answer to what the machine is for.

vs.q: What does Hatherley say to the Colonel that he instantly regrets?
opts: That the story about the fuller’s earth was a lie
That he would advise better if he knew the machine’s real purpose
That he intended to tell the police all about it in the morning
That the woman downstairs had warned him to leave
vs.why: He phrases it as an engineer being helpful and it is an accusation, and both men know it. “The instant that I uttered the words I regretted the rashness of my speech.”

vs.q: How does the Colonel answer that question?
opts: By offering him double the fee in return for his silence
By calling Ferguson to take him downstairs
By telling him the truth about the machine
By saying he shall know all about it — and locking him in
vs.why: “Very well, you shall know all about the machine.” It is a promise and a sentence at the same time. Then: a step backward, the door slammed, the key turned.

vs.q: Hatherley cannot help asking his question, even though he knows he should not. What does that say about him?
opts: He has no idea how much danger he is in
He is more frightened of being thought a fool than of Stark
He would rather understand a thing than be safe
He believes the Colonel will not dare to hurt him
vs.why: He has just been warned twice, he has seen the empty house and the metal crust, and he asks anyway, because the machine does not make sense and he wants it to. It is the same trait that brought him there for fifty guineas.

missions.name: Chapter 3 — pages 113 to 117
missions.blurb: The ceiling, the panel, the window and the cleaver

hi: the swish of the leaking cylinder
shapeless pulp
drowned my cries
a gush of hope

vs.q: What does Hatherley hear through the locked door?
opts: Ferguson arguing with the Colonel outside
The clank of the levers and the swish of the leaking cylinder
The woman calling his name from the stairs
A carriage being brought round to the front door of the house
vs.why: He hears the machine start, and he knows that sound: the swish is the leak he found himself half an hour before. The fault he was hired to diagnose is how he learns he is about to be killed.

vs.q: Why is Hatherley, of all people, in the worst position to hope the ceiling will stop?
opts: He is too weak from the journey to climb
He has no lamp and cannot see it coming
He had examined the press and knows its force
He is standing on the metal floor in the dark
vs.why: “As none knew better than myself, with a force that must grind me to a shapeless pulp.” He had put his hands on the piston. There is no comforting himself with not knowing.

vs.q: Why does shouting for help do him no good?
opts: The house is too far from any other building
The clanking of the levers drowns his cries
The Colonel had already left the house
The door is too thick for sound to pass through
vs.why: “The remorseless clanking of the levers drowned my cries.” The machine that is killing him is also the reason nobody can hear him — and the Colonel is the one working the levers.

vs.q: What is Hatherley thinking about while the ceiling comes down?
opts: Whether the panel in the wall will open
How he might jam the levers from inside
Which way to lie so that dying hurts less
Whether the woman will fetch help in time
vs.why: It is the most frightening paragraph in the story, and what makes it frightening is how practical he is: on his face the weight would come on his spine, and he shudders at “that dreadful snap.”

vs.q: The last sentence of the scene says his eye caught something that brought “a gush of hope” back. What had he seen?
opts: The key still turning in the lock
A light between two of the wooden boards
The lamp burning where he had set it down
The levers moving on the far side of the wall
vs.why: A thin line of yellow light between two boards — which is to say, a gap. He is saved by noticing something small at the exact moment he can no longer stand up straight.

hi: the floor and ceiling were of iron, the walls were of wood
a thin line of yellow light
the clang of the two slabs of metal

vs.q: What saves Hatherley’s life?
opts: The machine jamming before the ceiling reached him
The wooden walls, which had a panel in them
The woman stopping the engine from outside
The lamp setting fire to the boards
vs.why: “Though the floor and ceiling were of iron, the walls were of wood.” The part of the press that was not built to hold pressure is the part he gets out through.

vs.q: Why does the difference between iron and wood matter so much here?
opts: Wood muffles sound, so nobody heard him
Iron rusts, and the floor had worn thin
Wood burns, and he could have set it alight
Iron cannot be got through; wood can hide a door
vs.why: The floor and ceiling are the working faces of the press and they are iron. The sides only have to stand there, so they are boards — and a board can be pushed aside.

vs.q: What tells Hatherley how close the escape had been?
opts: The clang of the two slabs of metal behind him
The lamp going out as the panel closed
The sudden silence after the levers stopped
The pain in his hand as he fell through
vs.why: The panel shuts and he hears iron meet iron on the other side of it. He is lying half fainting in the corridor while the press closes on the space he was standing in.

vs.q: Who pushed the panel open?
opts: Ferguson, who had thought better of it
Nobody — the pressure forced the boards apart
Somebody outside the press, in the corridor
Hatherley himself, with the last of his strength
vs.why: The line of light “broadened as a small panel was pushed backwards” — pushed from the other side. He finds out who a moment later, when a hand plucks at his wrist.

vs.q: Think about the machine as its owners built it. Why would a press like that have a panel in its wall at all?
opts: So the men working it could get in and out quickly
So the piston could be reached for oiling and repair
So the room could be aired between uses
So water could be drained from the trough
vs.why: It is a workroom, not a trap — they used it every day to press metal, and a way in and out is ordinary. Stark locked the door and forgot what the men who work the machine rely on.

hi: remember your promise after the last time
He will be silent
You are mad, Elise
my thumb had been cut off

vs.q: Elise cries, “remember your promise after the last time. You said it would not happen again.” What does that tell you?
opts: That Stark had promised to give up the machine
That something like this has happened before
That she had helped a prisoner escape once already
That Stark had promised her a share of the money
vs.why: There was a last time. She is not guessing what Stark will do — she has seen him do it, and she got a promise out of him afterwards. Holmes produces the proof a few pages later.

vs.q: What reason does Stark give for not letting Hatherley go?
opts: That he cannot be trusted to keep a promise
That the police are already looking for him
That he has seen too much
That he knows the way back to the station
vs.why: “You will be the ruin of us. He has seen too much.” It is the plainest thing Stark says all night, and it is the only true one.

vs.q: What is the name Elise calls him by, and why is it worth noticing?
opts: Lysander — so the rank is invented
Fritz — so Colonel Lysander Stark is not his real name
Ferguson — so the two men are brothers
Jeremiah — so he has taken a dead man’s name for himself
vs.why: She calls him Fritz, in English, in front of a stranger. “Colonel Lysander Stark” is a costume — which is exactly why the porter at Eyford has never heard the name.

vs.q: Where was Hatherley when the blow fell?
opts: Standing on the sill with his back to the room
Hanging by his hands from the sill
Already falling towards the garden
Halfway across the bedroom floor
vs.why: “I was hanging with my hands across the sill when his blow fell.” His hands were the only part of him left in the room — which is how the story gets its title.

vs.q: When does Hatherley discover that his thumb has gone?
opts: At the moment the cleaver struck
Not until the doctor in town dressed the wound for him
Only when he woke in the morning
While running through the bushes, when the dizziness came
vs.why: “For the first time, saw that my thumb had been cut off.” He felt a dull pain, fell, got up and ran; it took a fit of dizziness to make him look at his own hand. Fear does that, and Doyle knows it.

missions.name: Chapter 4 — pages 118 to 120
missions.blurb: The hedge by the station, the advertisement, and Bradstreet’s circle

hi: neither house nor garden were to be seen
the very train station at which I had arrived
drenched with blood

vs.q: Where does Hatherley find himself when he wakes?
opts: In a field some miles from any road
In the garden he had jumped down into the night before
In the hedge beside the road, close to the station
In a bedroom at the inn at Eyford
vs.why: “Just a little lower down was the very train station at which I had arrived the previous night.” Of everything in this chapter, remember this: he wakes up next to the station he started from.

vs.q: What has become of the house and garden by morning?
opts: They are locked up and deserted
They are not to be seen at all
They are burning, and the gang have gone
They are full of police from Reading
vs.why: “To my astonishment, neither house nor garden were to be seen.” He did not walk away from the house — he was carried away from it, and that is a strange amount of trouble for the gang to take.

vs.q: He fainted in the bushes of a garden and woke in a hedge by the road. What must have happened in between?
opts: He walked there himself without remembering
The woman dragged him clear of the house
He was carried there while unconscious
The garden was beside the road all along
vs.why: Bradstreet asks about it on the train, and Hatherley admits “a confused memory of being lifted and conveyed somewhere.” Somebody moved him — and did not kill him.

vs.q: What condition is he in when he comes to himself?
opts: Unhurt except for the missing thumb
Wet with dew, his coat-sleeve drenched with blood
Bandaged already, with his hand properly dressed
Too weak to stand or move at all
vs.why: Dew on his clothes tells you how long he lay there; the sleeve tells you how much he had bled. He had been out for most of the night in the open.

vs.q: Waking next to the station is the most useful fact in the chapter. Why?
opts: It shows the gang wanted him to be found
It proves the house cannot have been far from Eyford
It means he can catch the first train to London
It shows the police station was closer than he thought
vs.why: They carried an unconscious man back to the station. Nobody carries a body twelve miles. Put this beside the horse that was still fresh and glossy, and the “hour’s drive” starts to look like a performance.

hi: Jeremiah Hayling
has not been heard of since
the last time the Colonel needed his machine overhauled
Then that explains what the girl said

vs.q: What does Holmes take down from the shelf?
opts: A railway timetable for the Reading line
A book of newspaper cuttings
A map of the country round Eyford
His index of London criminals
vs.why: One of the books in which he places his newspaper cuttings. Holmes’s filing is a kind of memory: he has been keeping this page for a year without knowing what it was for.

vs.q: Who was Jeremiah Hayling?
opts: A porter who vanished from Eyford station
A hydraulic engineer, aged 26, who disappeared
A clerk who once worked for the Colonel in London
The owner of the house before the gang took it
vs.why: “Lost on the 9th inst., Mr. Jeremiah Hayling, aged 26, a hydraulic engineer.” The same trade as Hatherley, and about the same age. The advertisement is a year old.

vs.q: What does Holmes say the advertisement represents?
opts: A rival gang working the same district
The reason the Colonel had to leave London in a hurry
The last time the Colonel needed his machine overhauled
The first crime the gang ever committed
vs.why: “That represents the last time the Colonel needed his machine overhauled, I fancy.” Said lightly, and it means that the last engineer who went out to mend the press never came back.

vs.q: Hatherley cries, “Then that explains what the girl said.” What had she said?
opts: That he should get away before it was too late
That the Colonel was not who he claimed to be
That there was no good for him to do there
Remember your promise after the last time
vs.why: Her promise makes sense the moment Hayling does. There had been a last time; she had made Stark swear it would not happen again; and Hatherley is standing in the place of a man who is still missing.

vs.q: Why is it so bad for Hatherley that the advertisement is a whole year old?
opts: It means the trail has gone cold since then
It means the police never managed to solve the first case
It means the gang have used the machine for years
It means the gang have done this before and got away with it
vs.why: A year has passed and nobody has found Jeremiah Hayling. Whatever happened to him, it worked — which is what Stark was counting on when he turned the levers.

hi: You are all wrong
I could lay my finger on it
no hills there
the country is more deserted there

vs.q: Each of the four men picks a direction. What does Holmes say to all four?
opts: That two of them may be right
That the south is the likeliest of them
That they are all wrong
That the map is too old to be trusted
vs.why: “You are all wrong.” “But we can’t all be.” “Oh, yes, you can.” They are arguing about which point on the circle to search; Holmes is telling them the circle itself is the mistake.

vs.q: What is Watson’s reason for guessing north?
opts: The roads are better that way
There are no hills, and the carriage went up none
There are quiet little villages up there
The country is more deserted in that direction
vs.why: Watson is reasoning from the evidence, and reasoning well — Hatherley never noticed the carriage climbing. It is a good argument built on the same bad number as everyone else’s.

vs.q: Bradstreet says south, Watson north, the plain-clothes man west, Hatherley east. What do all four guesses have in common?
opts: They all ignore what the porter said
They all assume the house is about ten miles out
They all rely on Bradstreet’s map being accurate
They all place the house near a village
vs.why: Four different directions and one shared assumption. Nobody questions the ten miles, so nobody can be right, whichever way they point.

vs.q: Holmes says quietly that he could lay his finger on the place. What has he been working from?
opts: The advertisement about Jeremiah Hayling
The map Bradstreet spread on the seat
Details in Hatherley’s own account
Information sent down from Scotland Yard
vs.why: He has been to no houses and interviewed nobody. Everything he has is what Hatherley told him in Baker Street — including the two things Hatherley did not know were important.

vs.q: You have read the same pages Holmes has. Which two facts should make you doubt the ten miles?
opts: The frosted windows, and the hour of the drive
The German books, and the empty upper rooms
The fresh horse, and waking up beside the station
The porter’s answer, and the cleaver in the passage
vs.why: A horse that had done twelve miles of heavy road would not be fresh and glossy, and nobody carries an unconscious man twelve miles to leave him by a station. Both facts are in your reading. Holmes has not been told anything you have not.
